title: Damped Harmonic Motion
short_intro: Damped harmonic motion is the oscillation of a system whose amplitude diminishes continuously with time due to dissipative forces such as friction or viscous drag. Energy is gradually converted into non-recoverable thermal energy, reducing the mechanical energy of the oscillator.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding of differential equations for damped oscillators, definition of damping coefficient, relaxation time, quality factor, and qualitative graphs of displacement-time under light, critical, and heavy damping.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped motion solutions, phase space trajectories, logarithmic decrement, and power dissipation in driven-damped systems.

prerequisites: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) kinematics and dynamics
Linear second-order homogeneous differential equations with constant coefficients
Conservation of mechanical energy and non-conservative forces

concept_notes.heading: Equation of Motion and Restoring Force
bullets: The net force acting on a damped oscillator comprises the restoring force (-kx) and the damping resistive force (-bv).
The parameter b represents the damping constant, depending on the medium viscosity and geometry of the moving object.
The resulting differential equation is m(d<sup>2</sup>x/dt<sup>2</sup>) + b(dx/dt) + kx = 0.

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Damping Regimes
bullets: Light damping occurs when the damping force is small compared to the restoring and inertial forces, leading to oscillatory decay.
Critical damping occurs when the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating.
Overdamping (heavy damping) occurs when the medium is highly viscous, causing the system to creep slowly back to equilibrium without oscillation.

concept_notes.heading: Logarithmic Decrement and Relaxation Time
bullets: Logarithmic decrement (λ) is the natural logarithm of the ratio of two successive amplitudes separated by one time period.
Relaxation time (τ) is the time interval in which the amplitude of a damped oscillator falls to 1/e of its initial value.
Higher damping leads to a larger logarithmic decrement and a shorter relaxation time.

concept_notes.heading: Quality Factor (Q-factor)
bullets: The Quality Factor Q is a dimensionless parameter characterizing how underdamped an oscillator is relative to its energy dissipation.
It is defined as 2π times the ratio of total stored energy to energy dissipated per cycle.
High Q oscillators exhibit very sharp resonance curves and slow amplitude decay rates.

derivations.title: General Solution for Underdamped Harmonic Motion
steps: Write the standard differential equation as d<sup>2</sup>x/dt<sup>2</sup> + 2γ(dx/dt) + ω<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>x = 0, where γ = b/(2m) and ω<sub>0</sub> = sqrt(k/m).
Assume a trial solution of the form x(t) = e<sup>rt</sup> and substitute to obtain the auxiliary equation r<sup>2</sup> + 2γr + ω<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> = 0.
Solve for roots using the quadratic formula: r = -γ ± sqrt(γ<sup>2</sup> - ω<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>). For underdamped motion, let ω<sub>1</sub> = sqrt(ω<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> - γ<sup>2</sup>).
Combine the complex exponential roots to form the general real solution: x(t) = A e<sup>-γt</sup> cos(ω<sub>1</sub>t + φ).

derivations.title: Logarithmic Decrement Derivation
steps: Write the expression for the amplitude at time t as a(t) = A e<sup>-γt</sup>.
Find the amplitude after one complete period T<sub>1</sub>: a(t + T<sub>1</sub>) = A e<sup>-γ(t + T<sub>1</sub></sup>).
Take the natural logarithm of the ratio of two successive amplitudes: λ = ln(a(t) / a(t + T<sub>1</sub>)).

formula_sheet.name: Differential Equation of Damped Motion
formula_sheet.variables: m = mass, b = damping coefficient, k = spring constant

formula_sheet.name: Quality Factor Q
formula_sheet.variables: E = total energy, ΔE = energy lost per cycle

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement vs Time for Three Damping Regimes
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three curves on an x-t plot: an exponentially decaying sinusoidal wave (underdamped), a single sharp non-oscillatory approach to zero (critically damped), and a slow sluggish asymptotic curve (overdamped).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Contrasts the oscillatory decay with fast non-oscillatory and sluggish returns to equilibrium.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification questions and matching regimes to b<sup>2</sup> vs 4mk relations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Envelope of Amplitude Decay
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal oscillation bounded symmetrically by upper and lower exponential decay curves +Ae<sup>-γt</sup> and -Ae<sup>-γt</sup>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that the oscillation frequency remains constant while the peak amplitudes decrease exponentially.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in problems calculating relaxation time and logarithmic decrement from successive peak values.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torsional Pendulum in Viscous Medium Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a disc suspended by a wire oscillating inside a fluid container, plotting angular deflection against time.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates practical measurement of damping constants and verification of exponential amplitude decay.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: VIVA and conceptual questions regarding laboratory determination of Q-factor.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 0.5 kg executes damped harmonic motion with a damping constant b = 0.1 kg/s and spring constant k = 2.0 N/m. Calculate its angular frequency of damped oscillation.
solution_steps: Identify given values: m = 0.5 kg, b = 0.1 kg/s, k = 2.0 N/m.
Calculate undamped angular frequency ω<sub>0</sub> = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(2.0 / 0.5) = sqrt(4) = 2.0 rad/s.
Calculate damped frequency ω<sub>1</sub> = sqrt(ω<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> - γ<sup>2</sup>) = sqrt(2.0<sup>2</sup> - 0.1<sup>2</sup>) = sqrt(4 - 0.01) = sqrt(3.99) ≈ 1.997 rad/s.

solved_numericals.question: The amplitude of a damped harmonic oscillator falls to 1/e of its initial value in 50 seconds. If the mass of the oscillator is 2 kg, determine the damping coefficient b.
solution_steps: Identify relaxation time τ = 50 s and mass m = 2 kg.
Use the relation for relaxation time: τ = 1/γ = 2m/b.

solved_numericals.question: For an underdamped oscillator, the amplitude decreases by 50% after 10 complete oscillations. If the time period is 2 seconds, find the logarithmic decrement and the damping factor γ.
solution_steps: Initial amplitude A<sub>0</sub>, amplitude after n = 10 cycles is A<sub>10</sub> = 0.5 A<sub>0</sub>.
Logarithmic decrement per cycle λ = (1/n) ln(A<sub>0</sub> / A<sub>n</sub>) = (1/10) ln(1 / 0.5) = ln(2) / 10 = 0.6931 / 10 = 0.0693.
Time period T<sub>1</sub> = 2 s, so damping factor γ = λ / T<sub>1</sub> = 0.0693 / 2 = 0.03465 s<sup>-1</sup>.

assumptions_and_limitations: The damping force is assumed to be directly proportional to the velocity (Stokes' drag), which holds strictly for small velocities in laminar flow regimes.
The restoring force obeys Hooke's law perfectly, neglecting elastic hysteresis and anharmonic terms at large amplitudes.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Damping changes the time period of oscillation significantly when damping is very small.
common_misconceptions.correct: In light damping (γ << ω<sub>0</sub>), the time period remains practically unchanged compared to undamped SHM.
common_misconceptions.why: The frequency correction term depends on γ<sup>2</sup>, which is negligible for small damping coefficients.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A critically damped system oscillates infinitely fast around the equilibrium position.
common_misconceptions.correct: A critically damped system does not oscillate at all; it approaches equilibrium asymptotically in minimum time.
common_misconceptions.why: By definition, critical damping eliminates oscillations while providing the fastest non-overshooting return.

quick_revision: Damping force acts opposite to velocity, causing exponential decay of mechanical energy and amplitude: x(t) = A e<sup>-γt</sup> cos(ω<sub>1</sub>t + φ).
Differential Equation of Damped Motion: m \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + b \frac{dx}{dt} + kx = 0
